articles.title: Judge allows NAACP lawsuit over xAI data center pollution to move forward
articles.summary: An NAACP lawsuit accuses the SpaceX-owned AI company of violating the Clean Air Act.
articles.full_text:
A federal judge denied a motion by xAI seeking to dismiss an NAACP lawsuit accusing the SpaceX-owned company of failing to obtain permits needed to operate the gas turbines powering its Colossus data center outside Memphis.

Suing on behalf of the NAACP, the Southern Environmental Law Center said the AI company had “installed and operated at least 35 combustion turbines and other sources of air pollution at the Colossus site without ever obtaining the necessary preconstruction or operating air permits.” It also accused xAI of violating the Clean Air Act. xAI sought to have the lawsuit dismissed, claiming that the turbines are exempt from permitting requirements because they’re mobile.

The company also argued that the plaintiffs did not have the standing to sue. “Because the plaintiffs have statutory standing under the Clean Air Act, because the combustion turbines are not ‘mobile sources’ under Mississippi’s [State Implementation Plan], and because the citizen suit provision does not violate Article II of the Constitution or the private nondelegation doctrine, the plaintiffs’ claims will proceed,” Judge Debra M.

Brown wrote in her decision .

Focusing on xAI’s claim that these kinds of citizen lawsuits are unconstitutional, Judge Brown wrote, “Because citizen suit plaintiffs sue on their own behalf, in their own name, and seek penalties that redress harm to themselves, they are not exercising the federal government’s executive power.” TechCrunch has reached out to SpaceX for comment.

In a statement , the NAACP’s director of environmental and climate justice Abre’ Connor described this as “another important victory in our effort to hold xAI accountable.” (A similar motion to dismiss from the Department of Justice was denied earlier this month ) “The courts have repeatedly rejected attempts by xAI and the DOJ to dismiss the NAACP’s Clean Air Act case, affirming our right to pursue justice for communities impacted by pollution,” Connor said. “Our position has been clear: xAI cannot operate gas turbines without the required permits.” The NAACP lawsuit is moving forward as public opinion seems to have turned sharply against data centers, with New York recently passing a moratorium on new data centers and other state and local governments considering similar measures.

The backlash also prompted Amazon and Microsoft to promise to stop using NDAs in their dealings with government agencies, and it could be a significant factor in the imminent U.S. midterm elections .

articles.title: OpenAI reportedly lowers funding target for new round
articles.summary: OpenAI’s latest funding round doesn't seem to be living up to expectations.
articles.full_text:
In Brief Posted: 9:12 AM PDT · October 31, 2026 Anthony Ha OpenAI reportedly lowers funding target for new round OpenAI’s latest funding round isn’t quite living up to expectations, according to multiple news reports.

OpenAI was previously reported to be raising $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation , and then at a $1.25 trillion valuation , ahead of a planned IPO.

But The Financial Times reported Friday that the company has subsequently lowered its funding target to $20 billion, with a first close that’s expected to be even lower than that.

The round will be led by a group of investors from the United Arab Emirates, the FT said.

A subsequent retail offering for wealthy individuals could bring the total funding amount to the $20 billion target.

A follow-up story in The Wall Street Journal offered more details, namely that the company has secured $11 billion so far, and that its fundraising efforts had met with a “tepid” response from some large investors.

TechCrunch has reached out to OpenAI for comment.

The company’s reported funding challenges could be blamed, in part, on bad timing, as Wall Street investors have become wary of heavy AI infrastructure spending , leading to a major sell off of tech stocks.

And Anthropic’s planned IPO could be facing challenges , too.

articles.title: 2026.44: At Long Last…
articles.summary: The best Stratechery content from the week of October 26, 2026 including Anthropic numbers, the end of the Internet as we know it, and autocracies then and now.
articles.full_text:
2026.44: At Long Last… Welcome back to This Week in Stratechery!

As a reminder, each week, every Friday, we’re sending out this overview of content in the Stratechery bundle; highlighted links are free for everyone .

Additionally, you have complete control over what we send to you.

If you don’t want to receive This Week in Stratechery emails (there is no podcast), please uncheck the box in your delivery settings .

On that note, here were a few of our favorites this week.

Finally, Some Anthropic Numbers.  Monday morning brought us Anthropic’s S-1, and not a moment too soon.

After four years of arguments about the economics at frontier labs, we now have some real numbers to sink our teeth into, and Ben did just that with his Update on Tuesday .

Come for that analysis, and then head over to this week’s Sharp Tech where we talked in depth about what Anthropic is telling investors, questions that remain unanswered, plus why the SEC forced Anthropic to help us understand Meta’s Muse bet . — Andrew Sharp The End of the Internet as We Know It (and I Feel Fine) .

Arriving on the heels of a handful of ominous cybersecurity incidents and with continued upheaval guaranteed, Monday’s Article made two distinct predictions .

First, the pressure applied by AI will eventually (or imminently?) rupture the global internet that we’ve come to know for the past 25 years.

But second, as society moves to more localized solutions and products, that may in fact be a welcome development for all of us who have come to accept degraded experiences throughout our technological lives.

As an avid group chatter who’s more or less abandoned public social media, I can certainly get behind the second take!  — AS Autocracies Then and Now.

On Sharp China this week, we began with an extended look at the climate of fear across the Chinese bureaucracy as Xi Jinping continues an anti-corruption crackdown that was absolutely necessary but may be going further than Xi’s earlier proponents ever expected.

Then, we turn to a glorious mess surrounding Mao Zedong and international soccer star Kylian Mbappé.

On both that episode and in this week’s Sharp Text , I make the point that connipitions like this one, anchored in a bizarre debate over Mao’s governing history, are evidence that rumors of a Chinese century have been greatly exaggerated.  — AS Presented by When I write about tech companies, I am often writing about businesses that depend on Stripe , because Stripe provides the foundation for Internet-native companies — including Stratechery.

Consider Substack: building Stratechery was complicated and involved gluing together disparate pieces; Substack made it easy by delivering an integrated offering.

One piece that was the same, however, was Stripe: Substack creators are also Stripe customers, as are creators on many other platforms.

Zoom out and the pattern repeats.

Fintechs can build entire business models around card programs without ever having to build the issuing and processing infrastructure underneath it.

AI companies can charge for what customers actually use, which is particularly important when usage also drives costs, without having to build the systems to track and bill for it themselves.

No business succeeds because of Stripe.

Stripe doesn’t answer the hard questions about what to build or whether anyone will actually use it.

But it does make more things practical to try.

Stratechery Articles and Updates The End of the Internet — The old Internet, where anyone could host a server is over, but it’s just the final blow in an ending that has been coming for years.

The future, though, is brighter than it appears.

Anthropic S-1, The Cost of Compute, Who Is Paying? — Anthropic’s IPO is finally here; the core business is very profitable, but competition may eat all of the profits, even as investors are set up for endless dilution.

Meta Earnings, Muse and the Frontier, Musebook — Meta’s earnings come in the context of Zuckerberg delivering on his promise; if investors believe in Muse they must support Meta’s spending on compute.

An Interview with Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar About the AI Religious War — An interview with Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar about AI diffusion and safety, forward-deployed engineer, and what the battle in tech is actually about.

Sharp Text by Andrew Sharp Kylian Mbappés Little Red Card — Surveying the biggest scandal in China this week, and another reminder that the CCP cannot get out of its own way.

articles.title: The Pulse: Anthropic kills the coding interview
articles.summary: AI is rendering the Leetcode-style interview pointless and now Anthropic has deleted it from its interview loop. Also: details of incident.io’s AI spend, Microsoft’s exit offer to engineers, and more
articles.full_text:
The Pulse The Pulse: Anthropic kills the coding interview AI is rendering the Leetcode-style interview pointless and now Anthropic has deleted it from its interview loop.

Also: details of incident.io’s AI spend, Microsoft’s exit offer to engineers, and more Gergely Orosz Oct 30, 2026 ∙ Paid 45 2 1 Share The Pulse is a series covering events, insights, and trends within Big Tech and startups.

Today, we cover: Anthropic kills its coding interview.

A team at the leading frontier AI company gets zero signal from DSA interviews and so has removed it from the engineering recruitment process.

The rest of the company, and other AI-native startups, could follow.

Details on incident.io’s AI spend and ROI.

The resiliency startup has slashed the amount it spends on AI; down from $4,500 per dev, per month, in August, to $1,600 now.

Amazon formally incorporates AI usage into SDE and SDM expectations.

AI has been placed at the heart of software engineering after the company found a correlation between AI usage and productivity.

Also, software development engineers (SDEs) and managers (SDMs) must be close to customers.

Microsoft issues new exit offers to engineers.

The tech giant has offered 60,000 employees the opportunity to quit by the end of the year.

But the exit package is not particularly tempting, and so the number of people who take it will surely be in the thousands, not tens of thousands.

Security incidents continue.

Since last week, incidents have continued to be reported, and that may not change for the foreseeable future. 1.

articles.title: Sam Altman sympathizes with mathematicians, but says OpenAI’s math onslaught won’t stop
articles.summary: After months of bombarding mathematicians with a relentless stream of AI-generated results, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says he sympathizes with researchers struggling to make sense of it all. But he has no intention of stopping - and hints there could be much more to come from the company's stockpile of discoveries. "I think, on net, […]
articles.full_text:
AI News Science Sam Altman sympathizes with mathematicians, but says OpenAI’s math onslaught won’t stop Altman says OpenAI has spent hundreds of millions on math — and has more discoveries up its sleeve.

Altman says OpenAI has spent hundreds of millions on math — and has more discoveries up its sleeve. by Robert Hart Oct 30, 2026, 1:01 PM UTC Link Share Gift Image: The Verge Part Of All the drama around AI’s takeover of mathematics see all updates Robert Hart is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow.

Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes .

After months of bombarding mathematicians with a relentless stream of AI-generated results, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says he sympathizes with researchers struggling to make sense of it all.

But he has no intention of stopping — and hints there could be much more to come from the company’s stockpile of discoveries. “I think, on net, the world deserves to understand how the universe works,” Altman said during an episode of the Cheeky Pint podcast released Thursday. “But I do have empathy for the method.” His comments mark one of the first times the OpenAI chief has directly acknowledged the company’s impact on mathematicians, following a string of genuinely impressive AI-generated results whose chaotic , poorly communicated rollouts have left researchers bewildered and struggling to keep up, even amid widespread excitement about AI’s potential as a tool for discovery.

Altman argued that the public’s right to new scientific knowledge “outweighs” the disruption caused by OpenAI’s releases, though he acknowledged the company needs to improve how it communicates its findings. “I feel unequivocal on this point: Humanity deserves fundamental knowledge, and we should not be sitting on a major fundamental science discovery,” he said. “The world deserves that.” Related All the drama around AI’s takeover of mathematics Researchers are getting tired of OpenAI gatekeeping its breakthroughs ‘Pure insanity’: Mathematicians will need years to make sense of OpenAI’s latest drop Mathematicians speaking to The Verge have repeatedly criticized OpenAI for how it announces its results, citing inadequate attribution, little context, and insufficient verification.

Researchers say this has left them doing the painstaking work of checking and making sense of their findings even as the company presses ahead with more.

This month alone, OpenAI has released hundreds of mathematical results , often with little more than brief writeups that researchers have described as poorly written and hard to follow.

Yet OpenAI is now facing criticism for doing precisely what Altman says it should not be: sitting on potentially significant findings.

Mathematicians and scientists speaking to The Verge this week said they are frustrated by what they see as OpenAI’s gatekeeping of research , following the announcement of three major breakthroughs in mathematics, physics, and computer science.

Details for one of the claimed results — involving Yang-Mills theory, the mathematical foundations of modern particle physics — have not been released publicly.

OpenAI says it is due to the recommendations of a hand-picked group of experts it consulted on how best to release it.

The practice runs directly counter to the advice of a previous group of mathematicians the company consulted , but forms part of what the company says is a new approach to communicating its findings.

On the podcast, Altman hints that OpenAI is sitting on many more mathematical discoveries than it has made public, too.

Asked whether the company has more than the hundreds of proofs they have already released, Altman replied: “We do.

Of course.” Altman also acknowledged that OpenAI’s pursuit of mathematical problems did “get out of control” for a short period of time, but said that was deliberate and necessary to probe the limits of its AI models.

He described an internal Slack channel called “Model Name-Hold My Beer,” where employees “were just throwing that at the hardest problems they could” to see how the models would perform.

Altman also estimated that OpenAI has spent in the order of hundreds of millions of dollars tackling mathematical problems, including around $10 million — “maybe a little more” — on its Navier-Stokes solution , one of mathematics’s legendary Millennium Prize problems.

The spending offers a glimpse of the vast resources AI labs are bringing to bear on scientific problems, raising concerns among researchers that they may be priced out of their own fields .

It looks like mathematicians and other researchers hoping for a breather may be out of luck.
